sources.title: Java Language Specification — Threads and Locks

stem: Two threads access the same ordinary variable concurrently, at least one access is a write, and no happens-before ordering connects them. What is this specifically called?

options.label: A data race
options.explanation: The accesses meet the memory-model definition of a data race: conflicting ordinary accesses without the required ordering.

options.label: A deadlock
options.explanation: Deadlock is a cycle or permanent wait for resources; these threads may continue running while corrupting the value.

options.label: A livelock
options.explanation: Livelock means threads keep reacting without making progress, not merely that conflicting memory accesses are unordered.

options.label: A benign race condition
options.explanation: “Benign” does not remove the data race; the memory-model classification follows from the conflicting unordered accesses.

stem: Two correctly synchronized withdrawals both inspect an account balance before either commits, so the business outcome depends on timing. Why can this be a race condition without being a data race?

options.label: Every race condition is defined as an unsynchronized byte access
options.explanation: Race conditions describe timing-dependent correctness more broadly; data races are the narrower memory-access category.

options.label: Synchronization can prevent simultaneous memory access while the multi-step business invariant still races
options.explanation: A data-race-free program can still interleave larger operations in an order that violates a higher-level invariant.

options.label: Mutexes make all multi-step business operations atomic automatically
options.explanation: A mutex protects only the state and duration covered by its critical section; split transactions may still race.

options.label: The database converts timing bugs into deadlocks
options.explanation: A database may serialize some operations, but it does not reclassify every timing-dependent invariant failure as deadlock.

stem: Several threads increment a non-atomic in-memory counter. Which basic design establishes mutual exclusion for that counter?

options.label: Give each thread its own mutex
options.explanation: Different mutexes do not exclude one another, so the counter remains concurrently accessible.

options.label: Notify a condition variable after every increment
options.explanation: Notification coordinates waiting; it does not itself serialize access to the counter.

options.label: Require every access to hold the same mutex
options.explanation: Mutual exclusion follows when all reads and writes participate in the protocol using the same mutex.

options.label: Mark the increment function asynchronous
options.explanation: Asynchrony changes scheduling but supplies no mutual-exclusion guarantee.

stem: A list is guarded by a mutex, but one helper reads it without acquiring that mutex. What is the core problem?

options.label: The mutex should be replaced by a longer name
options.explanation: Naming can document ownership but cannot synchronize an unguarded access.

options.label: The helper should sleep before reading
options.explanation: A delay changes likely timing and provides no ordering or exclusion guarantee.

options.label: The writer should notify twice
options.explanation: Notifications do not make an unrelated unlocked read safe.

options.label: The guarding discipline is incomplete
options.explanation: A lock protects an invariant only when every relevant access follows the same locking discipline.

stem: What does replacing a plain shared counter with an atomic fetch-add directly guarantee?

options.label: Each counter update is an indivisible atomic operation
options.explanation: Atomic read-modify-write prevents two updates to that atomic object from collapsing into one lost update.

options.label: All surrounding fields change in one transaction
options.explanation: Atomicity of one object does not automatically cover a multi-field invariant.

options.label: Threads execute in submission order
options.explanation: Atomic operations constrain observations, not scheduler order.

options.label: The counter can never overflow
options.explanation: Atomic arithmetic retains the type’s numeric range; it does not provide arbitrary precision.

stem: A queue stores atomic head and tail counters, but correctness requires head never to pass tail. Why may separate atomic operations be insufficient?

options.label: Atomic counters cannot be read
options.explanation: Atomic objects support reads; the issue is composing multiple operations and values.

options.label: Individual atomicity does not make the combined invariant atomic
options.explanation: Other threads can observe or create an invalid combination between separately atomic updates.

options.label: The counters must be converted to strings
options.explanation: Representation as text has no bearing on synchronization of the invariant.

options.label: Every invariant requires a counting semaphore
options.explanation: A semaphore limits permits but is not the universal mechanism for multi-value atomic transitions.

sources.title: Java Language Specification — Threads and Locks

stem: In a language memory model, what is the practical role of a happens-before relationship?

options.label: It proves the earlier action ran on a different CPU
options.explanation: The relationship is semantic and does not identify processor placement.

options.label: It measures elapsed wall-clock time
options.explanation: Happens-before is an ordering relation, not a latency measurement.

options.label: It guarantees ordering and visibility between the related actions
options.explanation: Happens-before constrains which writes a later action may observe and orders the actions for memory consistency.

options.label: It forces all threads to run sequentially
options.explanation: Only related actions receive the ordering guarantee; unrelated work may remain concurrent.

stem: A service owns eight identical database connections and must allow at most eight borrowers at once. Which primitive models this limit directly?

options.label: A condition variable with no predicate
options.explanation: A condition variable needs protected state and a predicate; by itself it does not represent eight available units.

options.label: Eight unrelated mutexes chosen randomly
options.explanation: Random lock choice can collide or leave resources untracked and does not cleanly represent a permit pool.

options.label: An atomic boolean
options.explanation: One boolean can represent at most a binary state, not eight concurrent leases.

options.label: A counting semaphore initialized with eight permits
options.explanation: Each borrower acquires one permit and releases it afterward, bounding concurrent holders to the resource count.

stem: What commonly distinguishes a mutex from a binary semaphore?

options.label: A mutex normally has ownership: the locker is responsible for unlocking it
options.explanation: Mutex ownership supports critical-section discipline, whereas semaphore permits can commonly be released by another participant.

options.label: A mutex always allows two holders
options.explanation: Mutual exclusion means at most one holder, not two.

options.label: A binary semaphore stores arbitrary messages
options.explanation: It stores permit state, not a message payload.

options.label: A semaphore makes memory immutable
options.explanation: Semaphores coordinate access; they do not change the mutability of data.

stem: Why should a thread waiting on a condition variable test its predicate in a loop?

options.label: The loop makes notification persistent forever
options.explanation: Condition notifications are not durable messages, and a loop does not turn them into stored events.

options.label: Wakeups do not guarantee the predicate is still true when the thread reacquires the lock
options.explanation: Spurious wakeups and competition with other threads require the waiter to re-check protected state before proceeding.

options.label: The loop prevents the mutex from being released while waiting
options.explanation: A condition wait releases the associated lock so another thread can change the predicate.

options.label: The loop guarantees FIFO waiter order
options.explanation: Predicate rechecking provides correctness, not a fairness order among waiters.

stem: A producer signals before a consumer begins waiting, and the consumer then sleeps forever even though work exists. What design avoids treating the signal as stored state?

options.label: Send the notification repeatedly on a timer
options.explanation: Repeated signals mask timing but still fail to define the state that permits progress.

options.label: Remove the mutex around the queue
options.explanation: Without synchronization, predicate checks and queue mutation can race.

options.label: Protect a durable predicate such as “queue not empty” and check it before waiting
options.explanation: The shared predicate records the condition; notification merely prompts waiters to check that state again.

options.label: Assume notify is queued until a waiter arrives
options.explanation: Condition-variable notifications generally have no durable memory when nobody is waiting.

stem: A condition wait returns even though no producer deliberately notified it. What must correct waiting code do?

options.label: Treat the return as proof that work exists
options.explanation: A wakeup is not evidence that the application predicate holds.

options.label: Discard the mutex permanently
options.explanation: The mutex is needed to inspect the predicate consistently with producers.

options.label: Increase the thread priority
options.explanation: Scheduling priority neither validates the predicate nor rules out spurious wakeups.

options.label: Re-evaluate the predicate and wait again if it is false
options.explanation: Condition APIs permit spurious wakeups, so only the protected predicate authorizes progress.

stem: Which access pattern does a reader-writer lock permit?

options.label: Multiple readers together, or one exclusive writer
options.explanation: Read mode can be shared, while write mode excludes both readers and other writers.

options.label: Multiple writers whenever no reader is waiting
options.explanation: Write ownership remains exclusive even in the absence of readers.

options.label: One reader only and unlimited writers
options.explanation: That reverses the intended sharing and exclusion rules.

options.label: Readers without any synchronization with writers
options.explanation: Readers and writers coordinate through the same lock to protect the state.

stem: Thread A holds lock X while waiting for Y; thread B holds Y while waiting for X. What failure is present?

options.label: Starvation without deadlock
options.explanation: Starvation need not involve a dependency cycle; here the circular wait identifies deadlock.

options.label: Deadlock
options.explanation: Each thread waits for a resource held by the other, forming a cycle with no possible progress.

options.label: A spurious wakeup
options.explanation: No condition wait returned unexpectedly; both threads remain blocked on locks.

options.label: Safe publication
options.explanation: Publication concerns visibility of initialized state, not circular lock dependencies.

stem: How does requiring every operation to acquire account locks in ascending account-ID order prevent transfer deadlocks?

options.label: It makes each transfer lock-free
options.explanation: Transfers still acquire locks and may block; the ordering only prevents cycles.

options.label: It guarantees every waiting thread equal CPU time
options.explanation: Lock ordering is a safety discipline, not a scheduler fairness policy.

options.label: It eliminates circular wait among those locks
options.explanation: A global order makes a cycle impossible because every dependency points in the same ordering direction.

options.label: It makes rollback unnecessary
options.explanation: Business or storage failures can still require rollback even when deadlock is prevented.

stem: Two polite workers repeatedly yield to each other, continually changing state but never entering the critical section. What is this?

options.label: Deadlock
options.explanation: Deadlocked workers are blocked rather than continually taking actions.

options.label: Data immutability
options.explanation: The symptom is lack of progress, not an immutable representation.

options.label: Safe publication
options.explanation: Visibility of constructed state does not describe repeated non-progressing retries.

options.label: Livelock
options.explanation: The workers remain active and responsive but their reactions prevent useful progress.

stem: A reader-preferred lock continually admits readers, so a waiting writer is postponed indefinitely. What liveness failure does the writer experience?

options.label: Starvation
options.explanation: The system as a whole progresses, but one participant is indefinitely denied the resource it needs.

options.label: Deadlock
options.explanation: Readers continue completing, so the whole wait graph is not permanently stuck.

options.label: A data race
options.explanation: The lock may synchronize memory correctly even while its admission policy starves the writer.

options.label: Atomicity
options.explanation: Atomicity describes indivisible actions, not indefinite denial of service.

stem: What does it mean for a component to be thread-safe?

options.label: It creates one operating-system thread per method
options.explanation: Thread creation strategy does not establish correctness of shared state.

options.label: It preserves its documented invariants under the concurrent uses allowed by its contract
options.explanation: Thread safety is a behavioral guarantee for permitted concurrent operations, not merely the presence of locks.

options.label: Every method must acquire a global mutex
options.explanation: Some thread-safe designs use immutability, confinement, atomics, or finer-grained synchronization.

options.label: Calls always complete in arrival order
options.explanation: Thread safety does not generally imply FIFO execution or fairness.

stem: Why is deeply immutable data easier to share across threads after safe publication?

options.label: Immutability forces all reads onto one core
options.explanation: Immutable objects may be read concurrently on many cores.

options.label: Immutability automatically waits for constructors
options.explanation: Safe publication is still needed; immutability alone does not establish the publication edge in every memory model.

options.label: No thread can race to change its state after publication
options.explanation: Once construction is visible and mutation is impossible, concurrent readers cannot conflict with later writers.

options.label: Immutable values never occupy memory
options.explanation: They still consume memory; the benefit is absence of mutation races.

stem: A mutable parser instance is used only by one worker and never escapes that worker. Which safety strategy is this?

options.label: Reader-writer locking
options.explanation: No shared lock is involved because the object is not shared.

options.label: Optimistic database locking
options.explanation: Version checks concern concurrent persisted updates, not single-thread object ownership.

options.label: Deadlock recovery
options.explanation: Nothing is waiting in a resource cycle.

options.label: Thread confinement
options.explanation: Keeping mutable state owned by one thread avoids concurrent access rather than synchronizing it.

stem: Which statement correctly separates safety from liveness in concurrent systems?

options.label: Safety says bad states do not occur; liveness says useful progress eventually occurs
options.explanation: Mutual exclusion is a safety property, while freedom from starvation is a liveness concern.

options.label: Safety measures speed; liveness measures memory use
options.explanation: Performance metrics are distinct from these correctness property classes.

options.label: Safety applies only to databases; liveness only to threads
options.explanation: Both kinds of properties apply across concurrent and distributed systems.

options.label: They are two names for mutual exclusion
options.explanation: Exclusion prevents overlapping access but does not guarantee future progress.

stem: Why can a bounded work queue provide backpressure between faster producers and slower consumers?

options.label: It makes consumers process each item instantly
options.explanation: Queue capacity does not change service time.

options.label: Once capacity is exhausted, producers must slow, wait, or receive rejection
options.explanation: The finite boundary converts consumer saturation into an explicit admission signal instead of unlimited buffering.

options.label: It guarantees no work is ever rejected
options.explanation: A bounded queue may deliberately block or reject when full.

options.label: It removes the need to measure queue delay
options.explanation: Queue occupancy and delay remain important saturation signals.

stem: What is the main overload risk of placing an unbounded queue before a fixed number of slow workers?

options.label: Workers become mathematically lock-free
options.explanation: Queue capacity does not determine progress guarantees of worker algorithms.

options.label: Every task is executed twice
options.explanation: Duplication depends on delivery semantics, not whether the queue has a bound.

options.label: Backlog can consume memory and make latency grow without enforcing admission control
options.explanation: An unbounded buffer hides overload temporarily while queued work and waiting time accumulate.

options.label: The queue enforces a strict deadline
options.explanation: An unbounded queue provides no automatic expiry or latency bound.

stem: For a blocking queue, which predicate should a consumer normally wait for under the queue lock?

options.label: A producer thread is currently running
options.explanation: Producer liveness does not prove an item is available.

options.label: A notification occurred recently
options.explanation: Notifications are hints to recheck state, not the state itself.

options.label: The queue has never been full
options.explanation: Past capacity says nothing about current item availability.

options.label: The queue is non-empty
options.explanation: That durable state determines whether removing an element is currently valid.

stem: What makes ordinary task cancellation cooperative?

options.label: The task observes a cancellation signal and exits at a safe point
options.explanation: The requester communicates intent; task code must stop work, unwind, and release resources.

options.label: The runtime always kills the thread at an arbitrary instruction
options.explanation: Asynchronous forced termination is generally unsafe and is not the normal cooperative model.

options.label: Cancellation rewinds every completed side effect
options.explanation: Previously committed I/O is not automatically undone by stopping future work.

options.label: Cancellation guarantees the task never started
options.explanation: A request may arrive after execution has already begun.

stem: What core lifetime rule does structured concurrency add to forked subtasks?

options.label: Every child runs on the caller thread
options.explanation: Structured lifetime does not require serial execution on one thread.

options.label: Child tasks are bounded by a lexical scope that joins or cancels them before it exits
options.explanation: The scope makes child lifetimes visible in program structure and prevents them from silently outliving the operation.

options.label: Children may outlive the process indefinitely
options.explanation: That is the unstructured lifetime problem the scope is intended to avoid.

options.label: Only one child may be forked
options.explanation: A structured scope is specifically useful for coordinating multiple related subtasks.

stem: A transaction locks an inventory row before checking and decrementing its quantity. Which concurrency strategy is this?

options.label: Optimistic concurrency control
options.explanation: Optimistic control normally proceeds without holding the conflict lock and validates at commit or update time.

options.label: Thread confinement
options.explanation: The database row is shared among transactions rather than owned by one thread.

options.label: Pessimistic concurrency control
options.explanation: The transaction prevents conflicting updates up front by acquiring a lock before acting.

options.label: Lock-free programming
options.explanation: The design explicitly waits on a database lock.

stem: An update succeeds only when the row version still equals the version originally read. Which strategy is this?

options.label: A counting semaphore
options.explanation: No fixed permit count is being acquired or released.

options.label: Pessimistic locking
options.explanation: The row is not held locked from the initial read through the update.

options.label: Condition-variable signaling
options.explanation: A database comparison predicate is not a thread wakeup mechanism.

options.label: Optimistic concurrency control
options.explanation: The writer detects a conflicting change through validation and can retry rather than locking throughout the edit.

stem: Multiple threads must allocate distinct sequence numbers from one in-memory counter. Which operation directly avoids lost increments?

options.label: An atomic fetch-and-add
options.explanation: The read-modify-write reserves and increments one value as a single atomic operation.

options.label: A plain read followed by a plain write
options.explanation: Two threads can read the same value and overwrite one another’s increments.

options.label: A condition notification
options.explanation: Notification does not update or serialize the counter.

options.label: A read-only lock acquired after incrementing
options.explanation: Locking after the conflicting update cannot protect it.

sources.title: Java Language Specification — Threads and Locks

stem: In Java, why is declaring an integer volatile insufficient to make count++ safe under concurrency?

options.label: Volatile values cannot be read by other threads
options.explanation: Volatile is explicitly used for cross-thread visibility.

options.label: The increment is a read-modify-write sequence, not one atomic action
options.explanation: Volatile supplies visibility and ordering for the individual accesses, but concurrent increments can still lose an update.

options.label: Volatile forces every access to throw an exception
options.explanation: The keyword changes memory semantics, not control flow.

options.label: Integer addition is forbidden in synchronized programs
options.explanation: Addition is valid; it simply needs an atomic or mutually exclusive update protocol.

stem: Thread A writes protected fields and unlocks mutex M. Thread B later locks M and reads them. Why should B observe A’s protected writes?

options.label: Both threads probably ran on the same core
options.explanation: Processor placement is neither required nor sufficient for language-level visibility.

options.label: The fields become atomic when placed near a mutex
options.explanation: A mutex does not change their types; visibility comes from following its protocol.

options.label: Unlocking M synchronizes with a later successful lock of M
options.explanation: The mutex edge orders operations before the unlock ahead of operations after the acquiring lock.

options.label: The scheduler flushes all process memory on every context switch
options.explanation: Memory-model guarantees are defined through synchronization, not an assumed global flush.

stem: A producer initializes an object, then stores true to an atomic ready flag with release ordering. What must the consumer use when observing true to see the initialized object?

options.label: A relaxed load followed only by a sleep
options.explanation: Delay supplies no acquire semantics or visibility guarantee.

options.label: A non-atomic read of the flag
options.explanation: Conflicting access to the flag would itself violate the atomic protocol.

options.label: A release load of the flag
options.explanation: Release constrains prior operations on a store; it is not the appropriate ordering for the consuming load.

options.label: An acquire load of the same publication flag
options.explanation: A release store read by an acquire load creates the synchronization edge that publishes prior initialization.

stem: Why is relaxed atomic ordering often sufficient for a telemetry counter whose value carries no publication meaning?

options.label: It preserves atomic updates without imposing cross-object ordering that the counter does not need
options.explanation: When only the numeric total matters, atomicity can be required independently from synchronization of other data.

options.label: Relaxed ordering makes increments non-atomic
options.explanation: Ordering and atomicity are separate; relaxed operations remain atomic.

options.label: Relaxed ordering returns an exact real-time global snapshot
options.explanation: Readers can see values at different times; relaxed does not create a wall-clock snapshot.

options.label: Relaxed ordering publishes every ordinary write in the process
options.explanation: It establishes no such general synchronization edge.

stem: What additional model does sequentially consistent atomic ordering provide beyond acquire-release ordering?

options.label: A guarantee that no thread is preempted
options.explanation: Memory ordering does not control OS scheduling.

options.label: A single total order of sequentially consistent operations consistent with thread order
options.explanation: This global order restricts how all seq-cst operations can be observed across threads.

options.label: Automatic atomicity for adjacent non-atomic fields
options.explanation: The guarantee applies to participating atomic operations, not nearby memory.

options.label: A deadline for every atomic operation
options.explanation: Progress and latency bounds are separate from consistency ordering.

stem: Why is compare-exchange commonly placed in a retry loop when updating an atomic value derived from its old value?

options.label: Compare-exchange always fails on its first call
options.explanation: It succeeds immediately when the expected value matches and no permitted spurious failure occurs.

options.label: The loop converts the atomic into a mutex
options.explanation: Retrying remains an optimistic atomic algorithm; it does not confer lock ownership.

options.label: Another thread may change the value between the read and attempted exchange
options.explanation: A failed comparison returns evidence of contention, so the desired value must be recomputed from the current state.

options.label: The loop guarantees wait-freedom
options.explanation: One thread can lose repeated races, so a retry loop alone does not bound per-thread completion.

stem: A compare-exchange sees pointer value A both before and after another thread changes A→B→A. What hazard can make the comparison misleading?

options.label: False sharing
options.explanation: False sharing concerns cache-line contention between distinct variables, not a repeated pointer value.

options.label: Priority inversion
options.explanation: Priority inversion arises from scheduling around a resource holder.

options.label: Spurious condition wakeup
options.explanation: No condition variable is involved in the atomic comparison.

options.label: The ABA problem
options.explanation: Equality of the final bits hides an intervening state change that may invalidate assumptions about the pointed-to object.

stem: Two threads update independent counters that occupy the same cache line and performance collapses despite no logical sharing. What is the likely cause?

options.label: False sharing
options.explanation: Cache coherence repeatedly transfers the line because independent writes share its hardware coherence unit.

options.label: A logical data race between the counters
options.explanation: The counters are independent and may each be correctly owned; the issue is physical cache-line placement.

options.label: Deadlock on the cache
options.explanation: Both threads continue making progress, so there is no circular wait.

options.label: Lost condition notifications
options.explanation: No waiter-notifier predicate is involved.

stem: A reader-writer lock admits new readers while a writer is already waiting. Under a continuous read stream, what can happen?

options.label: Two writers necessarily enter together
options.explanation: Reader admission policy does not remove exclusive write semantics.

options.label: The writer can starve
options.explanation: If fresh readers continually bypass it, the writer may never obtain exclusive ownership.

options.label: All readers deadlock with one another
options.explanation: Read holders are intentionally compatible with other readers.

options.label: The protected data becomes immutable
options.explanation: The lock policy does not change mutability.

stem: A server uses a 32-permit semaphore around an expensive downstream call. What overload property does this create?

options.label: Exactly 32 calls execute every second
options.explanation: A concurrency limit is not a throughput rate.

options.label: Every caller receives equal waiting time
options.explanation: Semaphore APIs need not promise strict fairness unless configured to do so.

options.label: At most 32 calls can be in the guarded region concurrently
options.explanation: Permit acquisition bounds in-flight concurrency independently of how many requests arrive.

options.label: Downstream latency cannot increase
options.explanation: The bound limits pressure but does not control the dependency’s service time.

stem: Why should a producer normally change a condition predicate while holding the associated lock?

options.label: Holding the lock stores notifications for future processes
options.explanation: Condition signals are not persisted messages.

options.label: It guarantees the awakened thread runs immediately
options.explanation: The scheduler may run the notifier or other contenders before the waiter reacquires the lock.

options.label: It prevents the producer from modifying the predicate
options.explanation: The producer holds the lock precisely so it can modify protected state safely.

options.label: It makes the state transition atomic with respect to waiters checking and sleeping
options.explanation: Using the same lock closes the race between observing a false predicate and entering the wait.

stem: After a condition-variable signal, why must the awakened waiter compete to reacquire the lock before assuming the predicate?

options.label: The signal makes it eligible to run but does not transfer lock ownership or reserve the predicate
options.explanation: Under common Mesa-style semantics, another thread may change protected state before the waiter resumes.

options.label: Signals terminate the waiting thread
options.explanation: A signal resumes waiting rather than ending the thread.

options.label: The waiter now owns every lock in the process
options.explanation: Condition wakeup concerns only its associated synchronization protocol.

options.label: Predicates are evaluated by the operating system
options.explanation: Application code owns and rechecks the predicate.

stem: A condition wait has a timeout. Why must code still inspect both the predicate and remaining deadline after it returns?

options.label: A timeout automatically commits partial work
options.explanation: Timing out does not imply any business transaction was committed.

options.label: Returns can reflect notification, spurious wakeup, or timeout, and none alone proves the predicate
options.explanation: Correct control flow derives progress from protected state and enforces the overall deadline across retries.

options.label: The first return permanently disables notifications
options.explanation: The waiter may continue waiting if its deadline and predicate allow it.

options.label: Elapsed time makes the predicate atomic
options.explanation: Timing does not supply mutual exclusion.

stem: Concurrent transfers sometimes lock the source row first and destination row second. Which change most directly reduces deadlock risk?

options.label: Use a random order for each retry
options.explanation: Randomization may reduce repeated collisions but does not prevent circular wait.

options.label: Hold the first lock while sleeping
options.explanation: Longer hold time increases contention and preserves the cycle.

options.label: Lock both rows in a deterministic global key order
options.explanation: All transfers then acquire overlapping resources in the same direction, breaking circular wait.

options.label: Read both rows without a transaction
options.explanation: Removing transactional protection can introduce lost updates and broken invariants.

stem: Two workers acquire one lock, fail tryLock on the second, release, and retry in perfect synchrony forever. Which mitigation targets this livelock?

options.label: Retry faster with no delay
options.explanation: Identical aggressive retries can reinforce the synchronized collision.

options.label: Replace tryLock with an unsynchronized read
options.explanation: Ignoring exclusion sacrifices safety rather than restoring correct progress.

options.label: Add another lock acquired in either order
options.explanation: An extra unordered resource expands the opportunities for cyclic contention.

options.label: Use randomized or asymmetric backoff before retrying
options.explanation: Breaking synchronized retries lets one participant advance while the other delays.

stem: What is a typical tradeoff of choosing a fair lock that favors the longest-waiting thread?

options.label: It can reduce starvation but also reduce throughput
options.explanation: Strict handoff limits barging and may increase scheduling and context-switch overhead.

options.label: It eliminates the need for mutual exclusion
options.explanation: Fairness determines admission order, not whether critical sections overlap.

options.label: It guarantees deadline scheduling
options.explanation: FIFO-like lock acquisition does not enforce real-time deadlines.

options.label: It makes critical sections run in parallel
options.explanation: The lock still admits one exclusive holder.

stem: Why can relying heavily on reentrant locking hide a design problem?

options.label: A reentrant lock permits unrelated threads to enter together
options.explanation: Reentrancy applies to repeated acquisition by the owning thread, not other threads.

options.label: Nested calls can obscure lock scope and preserve partially updated invariants longer than intended
options.explanation: Reentrancy prevents self-deadlock, but it can make ownership boundaries and callback hazards harder to reason about.

options.label: Reentrant locks cannot protect mutable state
options.explanation: They provide mutual exclusion like other exclusive locks.

options.label: Every recursive call creates a new operating-system process
options.explanation: Lock hold counts are bookkeeping, not process creation.

stem: In Java double-checked lazy initialization, why must the shared instance reference be volatile?

options.label: Volatile makes the constructor execute only once by itself
options.explanation: Mutual exclusion in the slow path still prevents duplicate construction.

options.label: Volatile prevents the object from being garbage-collected
options.explanation: Reachability, not volatile, governs ordinary object lifetime.

options.label: Volatile publication prevents observing the reference without the constructor’s preceding initialization effects
options.explanation: The volatile write and later read establish ordering and visibility for safely published state.

options.label: Volatile turns all instance methods into synchronized methods
options.explanation: It applies to accesses of the reference field, not arbitrary later methods.

sources.title: Java Language Specification — Threads and Locks

stem: What special guarantee do Java final fields receive when an object is properly constructed and its reference does not escape during construction?

options.label: All non-final mutable fields become permanently synchronized
options.explanation: The guarantee is not a blanket replacement for synchronization of later mutation.

options.label: The constructor may publish this before fields are assigned
options.explanation: Early escape defeats the properly constructed premise.

options.label: Final fields can be reassigned concurrently after publication
options.explanation: Final specifically restricts reassignment after construction.

options.label: A thread obtaining the reference can observe the initialized final-field values without an additional data race on those fields
options.explanation: The final-field semantics provide initialization safety, subject to the construction and escape rules.

stem: A thread-safe map exposes atomic get and put, but callers implement “if absent, then put” with separate calls. What can still go wrong?

options.label: Two callers can both observe absence and perform the compound action
options.explanation: Thread-safe individual methods do not automatically make a multi-call decision atomic.

options.label: The map loses type safety
options.explanation: Generic typing is unrelated to interleaving the compound operation.

options.explanation: Incorrect — It only bounds later attempts.

options.label: Unbounded retries amplify load and outlive the caller’s useful window
options.explanation: Correct — A budget limits resource consumption and end-to-end latency.

options.label: Deadlines make non-idempotent retries safe
options.explanation: Incorrect — Operation semantics and deduplication remain necessary.

options.label: Budgets synchronize every client clock
options.explanation: Incorrect — They constrain local behavior, not global time.

stem: Why should a durable-workflow activity that charges a card use a stable idempotency key?

options.label: Workflow history guarantees the payment API saw no request
options.explanation: Incorrect — A network response loss leaves the external outcome uncertain.

options.label: Stable keys make all cards share one charge
options.explanation: Incorrect — The key identifies one logical operation.

options.label: The activity may be retried after its result was lost
options.explanation: Correct — The external charge may have succeeded even when the workflow did not record completion.

options.label: Idempotency removes the need to authenticate the payment call
options.explanation: Incorrect — Authorization is still required.

stem: Why should an etcd disaster restore create a logically new cluster rather than let stale members rejoin automatically?

options.label: Snapshots contain no application data
options.explanation: Incorrect — They contain compacted cluster state.

options.label: Every old member is guaranteed empty
options.explanation: Incorrect — Stale disks can retain prior state.

options.label: Consensus accepts arbitrary histories when IDs match
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cluster identity and log history prevent unsafe merging.

options.label: Old members may carry incompatible cluster identity and history
options.explanation: Correct — A restored snapshot establishes a new authoritative membership and revision lineage.

stem: A service must remain available when one cloud data center loses power. What placement is the minimum direct protection?

options.label: Replicas in separate availability zones
options.explanation: Availability zones are distinct infrastructure failure domains, so a zonal outage need not remove every replica.

options.label: Two replicas on one larger VM
options.explanation: A larger host still leaves both processes inside the same host and zone failure path.

options.label: A second process in the same container
options.explanation: A sibling process shares the container, node, and zone, so it adds no data-center independence.

options.label: A longer health-check timeout
options.explanation: Changing detection time cannot preserve capacity after the only failure domain disappears.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes availability zones from regions in a typical cloud design?

options.label: Zones are global DNS names while regions are individual racks
options.explanation: DNS naming and physical rack boundaries are not what define the region-zone hierarchy.

options.label: Zones provide failure isolation within a region and usually lower inter-zone latency than inter-region links
options.explanation: Zones are separate facilities or facility groups inside one region, designed for isolation with regional connectivity.

options.label: Every region shares one synchronous control plane and one power supply
options.explanation: Regions are intended as separate geographic areas rather than a single shared power domain.

options.label: A zone can contain resources from several unrelated regions
options.explanation: A zone belongs to a region; it does not span multiple regions.

stem: A VM is replaced during recovery and its local temporary disk vanishes. Which design assumption was wrong?

options.label: Using a private network address for the VM
options.explanation: Private addressing affects reachability, not whether host-local bytes survive instance replacement.

options.label: Running the service without a public IP address
options.explanation: Public exposure is unrelated to persistence of the attached ephemeral device.

options.label: Treating instance-local storage as durable state
options.explanation: Instance-local storage is coupled to the host lifecycle and must not be the sole durable copy.

options.label: Selecting a recent machine image
options.explanation: The boot image version does not make runtime writes on temporary storage durable.

stem: A database needs a low-latency device it can format with a filesystem and update in place. Which storage primitive fits?

options.label: An object bucket
options.explanation: Object storage exposes whole objects through an API rather than a mountable block device with in-place writes.

options.label: A DNS zone
options.explanation: A DNS zone stores name records and cannot provide database pages to an operating system.

options.label: A container image registry
options.explanation: A registry distributes immutable image layers; it is not a mutable database device.

options.label: A block volume
options.explanation: Block storage exposes addressable blocks to the host, allowing filesystems and in-place database pages.

stem: Why is object storage a natural fit for large immutable backups?

options.label: It stores whole objects behind an API with durability independent of one compute host
options.explanation: Objects are accessed by key and persist independently of the VM that created them, matching backup lifecycles.

options.label: It exposes CPU cache lines directly to every VM
options.explanation: Object APIs do not provide processor-cache semantics or memory-coherent access.

options.label: It guarantees POSIX file locking across arbitrary clients
options.explanation: Object stores do not generally behave as a shared POSIX filesystem with advisory locks.

options.label: It rewrites small byte ranges without replacing an object
options.explanation: Whole-object operations, not arbitrary in-place byte updates, are the normal object-storage model.

stem: What is the main purpose of placing application servers in a private subnet?

options.label: Make every packet inside the subnet automatically encrypted
options.explanation: Subnet placement controls routing; encryption requires a separate transport or tunnel mechanism.

options.label: Avoid direct inbound reachability from the public internet while allowing controlled network paths
options.explanation: A private subnet omits a direct public ingress route, reducing exposed entry points while preserving routed access through approved components.

options.label: Eliminate the need for identity and authorization checks
options.explanation: Network location is only one boundary and cannot replace application or workload identity.

options.label: Guarantee that the servers run in different zones
options.explanation: A subnet is scoped to a zone on some clouds, but private routing alone does not distribute replicas.

stem: A stateful cloud firewall permits an inbound TCP connection. What normally happens to reply traffic for that connection?

options.label: The reply is always denied until DNS is updated
options.explanation: DNS resolution has no role in authorizing packets belonging to an established flow.

options.label: The reply requires an identical rule on every subnet ACL
options.explanation: A separate stateless ACL may need suitable rules, but that does not change the security group’s stateful behavior.

options.label: The established reply traffic is allowed without a mirrored inbound rule
options.explanation: Stateful filtering tracks the permitted connection and recognizes its return packets.

options.label: The connection is converted from TCP to UDP
options.explanation: Firewall state tracking does not change the transport protocol.

stem: Why must a stateless subnet ACL account for both directions of an allowed connection?

options.label: It automatically assumes all outbound packets are trusted
options.explanation: Stateless evaluation does not imply an unconditional outbound allow.

options.label: It authorizes users rather than network packets
options.explanation: A subnet ACL is a packet-filtering boundary, not a user identity policy.

options.label: It only applies after the application sends an HTTP response
options.explanation: ACL evaluation occurs at the network boundary regardless of application protocol stage.

options.label: It evaluates return packets independently instead of remembering the flow
options.explanation: Without connection state, the reverse packet must satisfy its own direction-specific rules.

stem: A cloud workload needs short-lived permission to read one bucket. What is safer than embedding a long-lived access key?

options.label: Attach an assumable workload role with narrowly scoped permissions
options.explanation: A workload role supplies temporary credentials and can restrict authority to the required bucket actions.

options.label: Store an administrator key inside the container image
options.explanation: Baked credentials are broadly exposed, hard to rotate, and grant far more authority than the workload needs.

options.label: Make the bucket public and rely on an obscure object name
options.explanation: Unpredictable names are not authorization and public access removes the intended identity boundary.

options.label: Reuse a developer’s personal credentials in production
options.explanation: Personal credentials couple service availability and audit trails to a human identity.

stem: Which description of a container is most accurate?

options.label: A complete physical server allocated to one application
options.explanation: A container is a software isolation unit and does not inherently reserve an entire physical machine.

options.label: An isolated process using host-kernel mechanisms and a packaged filesystem view
options.explanation: Containers isolate processes with mechanisms such as namespaces and cgroups while sharing the host kernel.

options.label: A virtual network that cannot execute processes
options.explanation: Networking can be namespaced, but execution of processes is central to a container.

options.label: A durable database replica created by the scheduler
options.explanation: Container execution does not itself provide durable storage or database replication.

stem: Why does a deployment pin a container image by digest instead of a mutable tag?

options.label: The digest increases the container CPU limit
options.explanation: Image identity and runtime resource allocation are independent controls.

options.label: The digest makes all image layers writable
options.explanation: Container image layers remain content-addressed; pinning does not alter their write behavior.

options.label: The digest identifies exact image content
options.explanation: A content digest is immutable for those bytes, making the deployed artifact reproducible and auditable.

options.label: The digest assigns the Pod to a particular node
options.explanation: Node placement is a scheduler decision, not a consequence of image addressing.

stem: What is the smallest deployable scheduling unit in Kubernetes?

options.label: A container image layer
options.explanation: An image layer is packaging data and is not independently scheduled as a workload.

options.label: A Service selector
options.explanation: A Service discovers endpoints but is not itself a unit of execution.

options.label: A namespace
options.explanation: A namespace groups and scopes objects; it does not represent a scheduled process.

options.label: A Pod
options.explanation: The scheduler binds Pods to nodes; containers that must share a Pod are placed together.

stem: Two containers must communicate over localhost and share a lifecycle. Where should they run?

options.label: In the same Pod
options.explanation: Containers in one Pod share its network namespace and are scheduled and managed as a unit.

options.label: In separate clusters
options.explanation: Separate clusters add isolation and make localhost communication impossible between the containers.

options.label: Behind unrelated external load balancers
options.explanation: External routing does not create a shared localhost or coupled lifecycle.

options.label: As two persistent volumes
options.explanation: Volumes hold data; they do not execute containers or supply networking.

stem: What does a Kubernetes Deployment primarily manage for a stateless application?

options.label: The physical wiring between cluster nodes
options.explanation: Cluster networking depends on infrastructure and plugins, not the Deployment controller.

options.label: A declared set of replicated Pods and their rollout
options.explanation: The Deployment controller reconciles ReplicaSets so the requested replicas and version are present.

options.label: Long-term retention of database blocks
options.explanation: Persistent data belongs in a suitable storage system; a Deployment manages workload replicas.

options.label: User identities in the cloud account
options.explanation: Cloud IAM principals are outside the Deployment workload controller.

sources.title: Kubernetes Services, Load Balancing, and Networking

stem: Pods are replaced and receive new IP addresses. What Kubernetes object gives clients a stable logical endpoint?

options.label: A ConfigMap
options.explanation: A ConfigMap distributes configuration values but does not route traffic to ready Pods.

options.label: A resource quota
options.explanation: A quota limits aggregate resource use and supplies no client endpoint.

options.label: A Service
options.explanation: A Service selects changing Pod endpoints and exposes a stable virtual address or discovery name.

options.label: A PodDisruptionBudget
options.explanation: A disruption budget constrains voluntary evictions rather than providing service discovery.

sources.title: Kubernetes liveness, readiness, and startup probes

stem: A process is alive but temporarily cannot serve requests. Which probe should fail to remove it from Service traffic?

options.label: The liveness probe
options.explanation: Liveness failure asks the kubelet to restart the container, which is unnecessary when the process only needs traffic withheld.

options.label: The startup probe after every request
options.explanation: Startup probes protect slow initialization and do not model recurring request readiness.

options.label: The image pull check
options.explanation: Image retrieval occurs before execution and says nothing about current serving ability.

options.label: The readiness probe
options.explanation: A failed readiness probe marks the Pod unready, so matching Services stop using it as a ready endpoint.

sources.title: Kubernetes liveness, readiness, and startup probes

stem: A server process stays running but is permanently deadlocked. Which probe can trigger a container restart?

options.label: A liveness probe
options.explanation: Liveness checks whether the running container should be restarted when it can no longer make progress.

options.label: A readiness probe only
options.explanation: Readiness can stop traffic, but a readiness failure by itself does not restart the container.

options.label: A topology spread constraint
options.explanation: Topology spread controls placement across domains and does not test process health.

options.label: A Service selector
options.explanation: Selectors choose endpoints by labels and cannot detect an internal deadlock.

sources.title: Kubernetes liveness, readiness, and startup probes

stem: A legacy application needs several minutes to initialize, but should still have an aggressive liveness check after startup. What helps?

options.label: A permanently failing readiness probe
options.explanation: Permanent unready state prevents traffic even after initialization succeeds.

options.label: A startup probe with enough time to succeed
options.explanation: While the startup probe is pending, Kubernetes suppresses liveness and readiness checks, avoiding premature restarts.

options.label: A larger Service port number
options.explanation: Port numbering does not change probe timing or initialization behavior.

options.label: A PodDisruptionBudget of zero replicas
options.explanation: A disruption budget concerns voluntary eviction and cannot protect a container from its liveness configuration.

sources.title: Kubernetes resource management for Pods and containers

stem: What does a Pod CPU request tell the Kubernetes scheduler?

options.label: The exact CPU time the process will consume every second
options.explanation: A request is a scheduling commitment, not a prediction of exact runtime utilization.

options.label: The maximum number of network connections the Pod may open
options.explanation: Connection count is not expressed by a CPU request.

options.label: The amount of CPU capacity to reserve when deciding where the Pod fits
options.explanation: Requests participate in placement so the scheduler does not intentionally overfill allocatable requested capacity.

options.label: The number of container images retained on the node
options.explanation: Image garbage collection is separate from workload CPU requests.

sources.title: Kubernetes resource management for Pods and containers

stem: What is the role of a container CPU limit?

options.label: It guarantees the container always receives that much CPU
options.explanation: The request, capacity, and contention influence guaranteed scheduling; a limit is an upper bound.

options.label: It chooses which availability zone hosts the Pod
options.explanation: Zone placement depends on nodes and scheduling constraints, not a CPU ceiling.

options.label: It encrypts traffic emitted by the process
options.explanation: CPU control does not supply transport encryption.

options.label: It bounds the CPU resource the container may use
options.explanation: The runtime enforces the configured CPU limit, typically by throttling when usage exceeds the allowance.

stem: Why use a PersistentVolumeClaim instead of writing important data only to a container filesystem?

options.label: The claim requests storage whose lifecycle is decoupled from one container instance
options.explanation: Persistent volumes let replacement Pods reattach storage according to the claim and storage class behavior.

options.label: The claim prevents every possible application-level data loss
options.explanation: Persistence infrastructure cannot correct destructive writes or missing backups in the application.

options.label: The claim makes a stateless Deployment stateful without code changes
options.explanation: Attaching storage does not define data consistency, locking, or application recovery behavior.

options.label: The claim assigns a public IP address to the Pod
options.explanation: Storage claims and network addressing are unrelated resource types.

stem: What does declarative infrastructure configuration primarily describe?

options.label: A required manual click sequence for each environment
options.explanation: An imperative click transcript is not a declarative model of the target state.

options.label: The desired end state of managed resources
options.explanation: The tool compares declared desired resources with known and observed state to plan convergence operations.

options.label: Only a log of completed production incidents
options.explanation: Incident records describe history rather than infrastructure that should exist.

options.label: A benchmark of application request latency
options.explanation: Performance measurements do not specify cloud resources and their configuration.

stem: Why does Terraform maintain state for managed infrastructure?

options.label: To store a second copy of every application database row
options.explanation: Terraform state is management metadata, not an application data backup.

options.label: To replace the cloud provider control plane
options.explanation: Providers still create and inspect resources through their APIs; state does not replace those services.

options.label: To map configuration resource instances to real remote objects
options.explanation: State records bindings and metadata so subsequent plans know which remote object each declaration manages.

options.label: To keep container logs indefinitely
options.explanation: Workload log retention requires an observability pipeline rather than Terraform state.

stem: Before changing shared infrastructure, what is the value of reviewing a saved Terraform plan?

options.label: It proves the new application has no runtime defects
options.explanation: An infrastructure plan cannot exercise all application behavior after deployment.

options.label: It guarantees no provider API will fail
options.explanation: The apply can still encounter permissions, quotas, conflicts, or provider errors.

options.label: It automatically backs up every managed data store
options.explanation: Planning shows resource operations but does not create application-aware backups.

options.label: It exposes the proposed create, update, replace, and destroy actions before apply
options.explanation: A reviewed plan makes the intended resource diff inspectable and can be applied as the approved artifact.

stem: What does least privilege require for a deployment service account?

options.label: Grant only the actions and resources needed for its deployment duties
options.explanation: Narrow authority reduces the damage possible from mistakes or credential compromise.

options.label: Grant administrator access but hide the account name
options.explanation: Obscurity does not restrict what a compromised credential can do.

options.label: Share one credential across development and production
options.explanation: Credential reuse expands the trust boundary and weakens attribution.

options.label: Allow every action and rely exclusively on audit logs
options.explanation: Logs help detection and investigation but do not prevent unauthorized operations.

stem: An identity policy allows an action, but an applicable policy contains an explicit deny for the same request. What is the decision?

options.label: The request is allowed because identity policies run first
options.explanation: Evaluation order does not let an allow bypass an applicable explicit deny.

options.label: The request is denied
options.explanation: In AWS policy evaluation, an applicable explicit deny overrides an allow.

options.label: The two policies cancel and create anonymous access
options.explanation: Conflicting statements resolve to denial, not removal of authentication.

options.label: The request is retried until the allow wins
options.explanation: Authorization is deterministic for the request context; retries do not alternate policy precedence.

stem: What is horizontal scaling for a stateless web tier?

options.label: Adding more CPU to the same single instance
options.explanation: Increasing resources on one instance is vertical scaling.

options.label: Moving logs from memory to disk
options.explanation: Changing log storage does not increase the number of serving instances.

options.label: Adding more serving replicas
options.explanation: Horizontal scaling increases the number of instances sharing the workload.

options.label: Replacing HTTPS with HTTP
options.explanation: Transport security choice is unrelated to horizontal capacity.

stem: A controller observes three replicas but the declared count is five. What should reconciliation do?

options.label: Rewrite the declaration to three without authorization
options.explanation: Observed shortfall should not silently redefine the user’s desired state.

options.label: Stop monitoring once it submits one API request
options.explanation: Controllers repeatedly observe because operations can fail and state can drift again.

options.label: Delete all replicas so both counts briefly become zero
options.explanation: Destroying healthy capacity does not converge directly or safely toward five replicas.

options.label: Create or request two more replicas and continue observing
options.explanation: A reconciliation loop acts on the difference between desired and observed state, then checks again.

stem: What operational property is commonly associated with serverless function platforms?

options.label: The platform creates and scales execution environments in response to invocations
options.explanation: The provider manages the execution fleet and can add environments as request concurrency grows.

options.label: The application team must rack every physical server
options.explanation: Serverless specifically abstracts host procurement and fleet operation from the application team.

options.label: Every invocation receives a permanently dedicated machine
options.explanation: Execution environments may be reused, created, and retired; permanent single-tenant hosts are not inherent.

options.label: Functions can keep durable state only in process memory
options.explanation: Process memory is ephemeral, so durable state must live in an external durable service.

stem: Why promote the same image digest from staging to production rather than rebuild it?

options.label: It guarantees staging and production have identical traffic
options.explanation: Artifact identity cannot make workload volume or user behavior identical.

options.label: It preserves artifact identity across environments
options.explanation: Promoting the digest ensures production receives the exact bytes that passed staging checks.

options.label: It removes the need for configuration management
options.explanation: The same artifact can still require environment-specific configuration supplied separately.

options.label: It makes rollback unnecessary
options.explanation: Even a reproducible artifact can contain defects or interact badly with production conditions.

stem: During a rolling Deployment update, what prevents a newly started but unready Pod from receiving normal Service traffic?

options.label: A liveness probe that succeeds immediately
options.explanation: Liveness only indicates whether restart is needed and does not prove the application is ready for traffic.

options.label: An image tag that contains the word stable
options.explanation: A tag name carries no runtime health signal to endpoint selection.

options.label: A readiness probe that has not yet succeeded
options.explanation: Unready Pods remain outside ready Service endpoints while the rollout controller can continue tracking availability.

options.label: A higher Pod priority
options.explanation: Priority affects scheduling and preemption, not whether the process is ready to serve.

stem: A Deployment must retain most of its serving capacity throughout a rollout. Which setting directly constrains how many desired Pods may be unavailable?

options.label: terminationMessagePath
options.explanation: The termination message location records exit information and does not set rollout capacity.

options.label: dnsPolicy
options.explanation: DNS behavior does not limit the number of unavailable workload replicas.

options.label: imagePullPolicy
options.explanation: Image pull behavior affects image retrieval, not the rollout availability budget.

options.label: maxUnavailable
options.explanation: The rollout controller uses maxUnavailable to bound unavailable desired replicas during the update.

sources.title: Kubernetes Services, Load Balancing, and Networking

stem: Several HTTP services need host- and path-based routing from one external entry point. Which layer provides that request-aware routing?

options.label: An Ingress or Gateway implementation in front of Services
options.explanation: Ingress or Gateway routing can inspect HTTP host and path data and forward to the selected Service.

options.label: A PersistentVolumeClaim shared by every Pod
options.explanation: Storage attachment cannot route HTTP requests by their headers or path.

options.label: A resource limit on the controller
options.explanation: CPU and memory bounds have no request-routing semantics.

options.label: A PodDisruptionBudget for each namespace
options.explanation: Disruption budgets protect availability during eviction but expose no HTTP entry point.

sources.title: Kubernetes Services, Load Balancing, and Networking

stem: A Service has no ready endpoints even though Pods are running. What should be checked first?

options.label: Whether every Pod uses host networking
options.explanation: Ordinary Services work with Pod networking and do not require host-network mode.

options.label: Whether its selector matches the Pods and those Pods are ready
options.explanation: Service discovery depends on label selection and endpoint readiness; either mismatch can leave the endpoint set empty.

options.label: Whether the namespace has a PersistentVolume
options.explanation: A Service can route to stateless Pods without any volume.

options.label: Whether the cluster has exactly one node
options.explanation: Service endpoint selection is not contingent on a single-node topology.

stem: GPU nodes are reserved for approved workloads, and ordinary Pods should not land there. Which mechanism expresses the repulsion side of that policy?

options.label: A liveness probe on ordinary Pods
options.explanation: Process-health checks do not influence whether a Pod is eligible for GPU nodes.

options.label: A Service without a selector
options.explanation: Endpoint discovery has no effect on scheduler placement.

options.label: A taint on the GPU nodes
options.explanation: A NoSchedule taint rejects Pods that lack the matching toleration, protecting the specialized node pool.

options.label: A larger container image
options.explanation: Image size is not an authorization or placement constraint for the node pool.

stem: A Pod tolerates a node taint. What does that toleration establish by itself?

options.label: It reserves the entire node exclusively for that Pod
options.explanation: A toleration neither requests exclusivity nor prevents other eligible Pods from sharing the node.

options.label: It bypasses all CPU and memory fit checks
options.explanation: The scheduler still evaluates resource requests and other placement constraints.

options.label: It grants cloud API permissions to the Pod
options.explanation: Scheduler tolerations do not modify workload identity or IAM policy.

options.label: It makes the Pod eligible for the tainted node, but does not force placement there
options.explanation: Toleration removes a repulsion constraint; affinity or node selection is needed to attract the Pod.

stem: Replicas should be distributed across zones instead of clustering in one zone. What expresses this intent directly?

options.label: A topology spread constraint using the zone topology key
options.explanation: Topology spread constrains skew among eligible domains identified by the selected topology key.

options.label: A startup probe with a long timeout
options.explanation: Startup health timing cannot distribute replicas across failure domains.

options.label: A Service type change from ClusterIP to NodePort
options.explanation: Service exposure changes traffic entry, not Pod placement balance.

options.label: A larger ephemeral-storage limit
options.explanation: Storage allowance does not encode zonal diversity.

stem: A latency-sensitive helper should run in the same zone as Pods carrying a particular label. Which scheduler feature fits?

options.label: A network policy allowing all egress
options.explanation: Network policy controls allowed connections and does not request colocation.

options.label: Pod affinity scoped to the zone topology key
options.explanation: Pod affinity can attract the helper to a topology domain containing matching Pods.

options.label: A liveness probe against the peer
options.explanation: Health checking a peer cannot influence initial scheduler placement.

options.label: A PersistentVolume reclaim policy
options.explanation: Volume cleanup behavior does not express workload affinity.

stem: A critical Pod cannot fit, but lower-priority Pods occupy suitable nodes. What may Kubernetes preemption do?

options.label: Increase the physical memory installed in a node
options.explanation: The scheduler cannot alter server hardware to satisfy the request.

options.label: Ignore all topology and resource constraints for the critical Pod
options.explanation: Priority does not make an otherwise infeasible placement valid.

options.label: Evict selected lower-priority Pods so the critical Pod can schedule
options.explanation: Preemption can nominate a node and remove lower-priority occupants when that makes the pending Pod feasible.

options.label: Convert the critical Pod into a Service
options.explanation: A Service is a networking abstraction and cannot replace the pending workload.

sources.title: Kubernetes resource management for Pods and containers

stem: Actual CPU use is low, yet a pending Pod cannot fit because nodes have little unallocated requested CPU. Why?

options.label: Kubernetes schedules only one Pod per node
options.explanation: Nodes normally host many Pods when constraints and requested resources fit.

options.label: Readiness probes reserve all remaining CPU
options.explanation: Probe execution does not automatically consume every unrequested CPU unit.

options.label: Services prevent Pods from sharing nodes
options.explanation: Service membership and node colocation are independent.

options.label: Scheduling capacity is evaluated from requests, not momentary utilization
options.explanation: Requests are the scheduler’s capacity commitments, so idle usage does not erase already reserved fit.

sources.title: Kubernetes resource management for Pods and containers

stem: A container repeatedly exceeds its memory limit. What failure should operators expect?

options.label: The container process can be killed for out-of-memory use
options.explanation: Memory limits are enforced reactively, and a process exceeding the cgroup allowance can be terminated.

options.label: The scheduler automatically doubles the limit permanently
options.explanation: A static Pod specification is not rewritten merely because the process exceeded its bound.

options.label: The Service allocates a second IP address to hold memory
options.explanation: Network addressing cannot supply process memory.

options.label: The image registry stores the excess heap
options.explanation: Registry storage contains image layers and is not runtime swap for a container.

stem: A node drain uses the Eviction API, but evicting another replica would violate a PodDisruptionBudget. What should happen?

options.label: The Pod is immediately deleted because drains bypass every budget
options.explanation: API-initiated eviction is precisely the path on which a PDB can constrain the drain.

options.label: The eviction is rejected or delayed until the budget permits it
options.explanation: The Eviction API checks the budget and protects the configured minimum availability from voluntary disruption.

options.label: The Pod is moved live without termination
options.explanation: Kubernetes generally terminates and recreates Pods rather than live-migrating their processes.

options.label: The node receives a larger CPU limit
options.explanation: A disruption budget does not resize the node or workload.

stem: What can a PodDisruptionBudget not prevent?

options.label: An administrator eviction submitted through the Eviction API
options.explanation: That voluntary operation is a principal use case for budget enforcement.

options.label: A controlled node drain that honors eviction responses
options.explanation: A compliant drain retries when the PDB temporarily rejects eviction.

options.label: A node disappearing because of hardware failure
options.explanation: PDBs constrain voluntary evictions; involuntary infrastructure loss can still remove Pods and counts against availability.

options.label: A cluster autoscaler drain using the eviction mechanism
options.explanation: Voluntary scale-down normally has to respect disruption budgets.

stem: A replicated database requires stable ordinal identities and one persistent volume per replica. Which workload controller is designed for this?

options.label: A bare ServiceAccount
options.explanation: A ServiceAccount supplies workload identity and manages neither replicas nor volumes.

options.label: A DaemonSet with one shared writable volume
options.explanation: DaemonSets target nodes, and a shared write volume does not create stable database replica identity.

options.label: A ConfigMap mounted as storage
options.explanation: ConfigMaps are for configuration data and are not durable database volumes.

options.label: A StatefulSet
options.explanation: StatefulSets preserve ordered Pod identities and can create stable per-Pod claims from volume claim templates.

stem: A zonal block volume can attach only within its zone. What must scheduling account for when a Pod claims it?

options.label: The Pod must be placed on a compatible node in the volume’s topology
options.explanation: The storage and scheduler constraints must align because the provider cannot attach that zonal device elsewhere.

options.label: The Pod must use the host’s public IP address
options.explanation: Public addressing has no bearing on block-volume attachment locality.

options.label: The volume must be converted into a container image
options.explanation: Images package executable files; they do not replace a mutable persistent volume.

options.label: The Service must route only UDP traffic
options.explanation: Transport protocol selection is unrelated to storage-zone compatibility.

stem: A namespace needs deny-by-default ingress for selected Pods. What is the essential NetworkPolicy pattern?

options.label: Create a Service with no ports
options.explanation: Service configuration does not establish a deny-by-default packet policy for direct Pod traffic.

options.label: Select those Pods for ingress while allowing no ingress peers
options.explanation: Once a Pod is isolated for ingress, only traffic explicitly allowed by applicable policies is admitted.

options.label: Remove every readiness probe
options.explanation: Probe presence does not define network authorization.

options.label: Set each container CPU request to zero
options.explanation: CPU scheduling values cannot block incoming connections.

stem: Two NetworkPolicies select the same Pod and each allows a different ingress source. How are their allowed sources combined?

options.label: Only the alphabetically first policy is evaluated
options.explanation: Policy names do not determine precedence.

options.label: The policies cancel and isolate all traffic
options.explanation: Multiple selects do not negate one another; their permitted sets accumulate.

options.label: Additively: traffic allowed by either applicable policy is allowed
options.explanation: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies compose allowed connections as a union rather than using rule order.

options.label: The newest policy replaces the older policy
options.explanation: NetworkPolicy is not an ordered last-write-wins firewall rule list.

stem: Why require application containers to run as non-root where possible?

options.label: It encrypts every volume automatically
options.explanation: User identity does not provide storage encryption.

options.label: It guarantees the container has no kernel attack surface
options.explanation: Containers still share a kernel; non-root narrows privilege but does not eliminate kernel exposure.

options.label: It makes resource limits unnecessary
options.explanation: CPU and memory controls address resource isolation separately from user privileges.

options.label: It reduces the privileges available after a container compromise
options.explanation: A non-root process has less ambient authority inside its isolation boundary and limits common escalation paths.

stem: Why is putting a password in a Kubernetes Secret better than embedding it in an image, yet still not sufficient by itself?

options.label: It separates secret delivery from the artifact, but access control and encryption still require configuration
options.explanation: Secrets avoid baking credentials into distributable layers, while RBAC, storage encryption, and workload access remain separate responsibilities.

options.label: A Secret makes the password public only inside DNS
options.explanation: Secrets are API objects and are not intentionally published through DNS.

options.label: A Secret prevents every privileged node process from reading it
options.explanation: Node-level privilege and workload compromise remain part of the threat model.

options.label: A Secret rotates the upstream credential on every Pod start
options.explanation: Kubernetes stores and delivers the value; rotation of the external credential is not automatic.

stem: A CPU-utilization HPA has no usable CPU requests on its target Pods. Why is that a problem?

options.label: The HPA needs a public load balancer before reading metrics
options.explanation: Metric collection and scaling do not require public exposure.

options.label: Utilization is calculated relative to requested CPU, so the controller lacks the denominator
options.explanation: Resource utilization targets depend on requests; missing requests can prevent the HPA from producing the intended scale recommendation.

options.label: CPU limits must always equal the node’s total CPU
options.explanation: Neither HPA operation nor Pod configuration requires one container to claim the whole node.

options.label: A StatefulSet is mandatory for horizontal scaling
options.explanation: HPAs can target scalable workload resources such as Deployments.

stem: What does a HorizontalPodAutoscaler change when observed demand exceeds its target?
