options.explanation: Incorrect — The application reads signal information in user space.

stem: What does a PID namespace virtualize?

options.label: CPU time accounting
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cgroup controllers handle CPU resources.

options.label: File contents in page cache
options.explanation: Incorrect — The cache is not per PID namespace.

options.label: Process ID visibility and numbering
options.explanation: Correct — Processes can see a namespace-specific process tree.

options.label: Java heap generations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Runtime GC layout is unrelated.

stem: What does a mount namespace isolate?

options.label: Physical disk failure
options.explanation: Incorrect — Isolation cannot prevent device failure.

options.label: User-space heap addresses
options.explanation: Incorrect — Address spaces are per process.

options.label: CPU instruction ordering
options.explanation: Incorrect — Memory models govern ordering.

options.label: The set of mounts visible to processes
options.explanation: Correct — Mount and unmount changes can be scoped to the namespace.

stem: What useful mapping can a user namespace provide?

options.label: A process can be namespace root while mapped to an unprivileged host user
options.explanation: Correct — Capabilities are scoped to the namespace and mappings.

options.label: Host root access without restrictions
options.explanation: Incorrect — Namespace root is not automatically global root.

options.label: Unlimited cgroup memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resource limits remain separate.

options.label: A private CPU cache
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hardware cache is not namespaced.

stem: What does cgroup v2 memory.max define?

options.label: A minimum CPU share
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU controllers use other files.

options.label: A hard memory usage limit for the cgroup
options.explanation: Correct — Crossing it invokes reclaim and possibly cgroup OOM handling.

options.label: A mount namespace root
options.explanation: Incorrect — Filesystem views are namespace concerns.

options.label: The maximum file descriptor number
options.explanation: Incorrect — Descriptor limits are different controls.

stem: What does cgroup v2 cpu.weight influence?

options.label: A hard byte limit on memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — The memory controller supplies that.

options.label: Network namespace membership
options.explanation: Incorrect — Namespaces isolate network views.

options.label: Relative CPU distribution under contention
options.explanation: Correct — Weights guide proportional scheduling among sibling cgroups.

options.label: File sync frequency
options.explanation: Incorrect — Writeback durability is separate.

stem: What can happen when a cgroup cannot reclaim enough memory under its hard limit?

options.label: The group gains unlimited host memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — The hard limit is enforced.

options.label: Every host process is necessarily killed
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cgroup-scoped OOM aims to contain impact.

options.label: All pages become read-only
options.explanation: Incorrect — Protection flags are unrelated.

options.label: The kernel invokes OOM handling within that cgroup
options.explanation: Correct — A task may be killed to restore the limit.

stem: What tradeoff does increasing GOGC usually make in a steady Go workload?

options.label: More memory between collections for less frequent GC CPU work
options.explanation: Correct — A larger heap-growth target triggers collection less often.

options.label: Less memory and more frequent collections
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is the direction of lowering GOGC.

options.label: No effect on runtime behavior
options.explanation: Incorrect — GOGC configures the heap target.

options.label: It disables allocation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Programs continue allocating.

stem: Why do concurrent collectors still need brief stop-the-world phases?

options.label: Concurrent marking never runs with applications
options.explanation: Incorrect — Most tracing can overlap execution.

options.label: Some root and phase-transition work needs a stable view
options.explanation: Correct — Safepoints coordinate mutators for bounded critical collector work.

options.label: Stopping threads makes unreachable objects live
options.explanation: Incorrect — Pauses support bookkeeping, not liveness changes.

options.label: The OS requires GC before every syscall
options.explanation: Incorrect — No such requirement exists.

stem: What observation motivates generational garbage collection?

options.label: Every old object is unreachable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Long-lived objects can remain live.

options.label: Object age equals security privilege
options.explanation: Incorrect — Age is a collection heuristic.

options.label: Most newly allocated objects die young
options.explanation: Correct — Frequent collection of young regions reclaims much garbage cheaply.

options.label: Young objects never reference old objects
options.explanation: Incorrect — Collectors need remembered sets for cross-generation references.

stem: Why can a JIT-managed service run slower immediately after startup?

options.label: The CPU cannot execute machine code after boot
options.explanation: Incorrect — Machine code executes from the beginning.

options.label: Virtual memory is disabled temporarily
options.explanation: Incorrect — Address translation remains active.

options.label: The filesystem permanently bypasses cache
options.explanation: Incorrect — Startup I/O cache state is separate from JIT tiering.

options.label: Code has not yet accumulated profiles or reached optimized tiers
options.explanation: Correct — Warm-up includes interpretation, baseline compilation, and profiling.

stem: What is JIT deoptimization?

options.label: Returning optimized code to a more general execution form when assumptions fail
options.explanation: Correct — The runtime reconstructs state and continues safely.

options.label: Deleting application source files
options.explanation: Incorrect — Deoptimization changes execution tiers.

options.label: Turning off virtual memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — It is a compiler-runtime action.

options.label: Forcing every thread onto one CPU
options.explanation: Incorrect — Scheduling affinity is separate.

stem: What causes false sharing?

options.label: Threads read one immutable value
options.explanation: Incorrect — Read-only sharing usually avoids invalidation traffic.

options.label: Threads modify independent variables on the same cache line
options.explanation: Correct — Coherence transfers the line despite no logical data sharing.

options.label: Processes use separate physical machines
options.explanation: Incorrect — False sharing occurs through a shared coherent cache hierarchy.

options.label: A page is absent from RAM
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is a page fault.

stem: What does a release store paired with an acquire load of its value establish?

options.label: All CPUs stop permanently
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ordering does not halt execution.

options.label: Every unrelated atomic has one global timestamp
options.explanation: Incorrect — Acquire-release is scoped by synchronization relationships.

options.label: Earlier writes before release become visible after acquire
options.explanation: Correct — The synchronization edge orders surrounding memory operations.

options.label: The variable stops being atomic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Both operations remain atomic.

stem: Why can fork of a huge process still cause latency even before many pages are copied?

options.label: fork copies no kernel state at all
options.explanation: Incorrect — It constructs a child task and address-space structures.

options.label: Every page is written to disk first
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is not a fork requirement.

options.label: The child must immediately garbage-collect parent memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — GC is runtime-specific.

options.label: The kernel must duplicate and manage substantial page-table metadata
options.explanation: Correct — COW avoids copying contents but not all mapping work.

stem: Why can transparent huge pages hurt a latency-sensitive workload despite fewer TLB misses?

options.label: Allocation, compaction, and splitting can create latency spikes
options.explanation: Correct — Huge-page management adds larger-granularity work.

options.label: Huge pages cannot be mapped by CPUs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Supported CPUs translate them normally.

options.label: They force every file write to fsync
options.explanation: Incorrect — Memory-page size is unrelated to durability.

options.label: They disable all cache locality
options.explanation: Incorrect — They may improve translation locality.

stem: A mapped file is truncated below a page the process later accesses. What failure can occur?

options.label: The kernel extends the file silently
options.explanation: Incorrect — Mapped access beyond the object does not define extension.

options.label: The access can raise SIGBUS
options.explanation: Correct — The mapping address exists but no longer has backing object data.

options.label: The process receives SIGKILL by definition
options.explanation: Incorrect — SIGBUS is the documented mapping fault.

options.label: The page becomes anonymous memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — The file-backed mapping does not automatically convert.

stem: Why can a buffered writer suddenly stall after many fast writes?

options.label: Page cache guarantees constant latency
options.explanation: Incorrect — Writeback produces variable latency.

options.label: The scheduler converts writes to signals
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dirty-page throttling waits for writeback; it does not convert writes into signals.

options.label: Dirty-page limits can throttle it while writeback catches up
options.explanation: Correct — Buffered I/O defers storage cost until memory pressure or thresholds.

options.label: Every dirty page is already durable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dirty means modified but not yet persisted.

stem: Why must an application check fsync’s return value?

options.label: fsync returns the file’s contents
options.explanation: Incorrect — It returns success or error status.

options.label: Ignoring errors makes data more durable
options.explanation: Incorrect — It hides failed persistence.

options.label: The call always succeeds on regular files
options.explanation: Incorrect — Storage and filesystem errors are possible.

options.label: Delayed writeback errors may surface only at synchronization
options.explanation: Correct — Earlier buffered writes can appear successful before storage failure is reported.

stem: For a crash-safe replace using a temporary file, what sequence protects both contents and name?

options.label: fsync the temp file, rename it, then fsync the directory
options.explanation: Correct — The sequence persists data before atomically publishing and then persists the namespace update.

options.label: rename first and never sync anything
options.explanation: Incorrect — Visibility does not ensure crash durability.

options.label: unlink both paths before writing
options.explanation: Incorrect — That creates an avoidable missing-file window.

options.label: Only sync an unrelated descriptor
options.explanation: Incorrect — Durability must cover the relevant file and directory.

stem: What benefit can registered io_uring buffers provide?

options.label: Allow the application to free memory before completion
options.explanation: Incorrect — Registered memory must remain valid while registered and in use.

options.label: Avoid repeated buffer pinning and mapping work for recurring I/O
options.explanation: Correct — Registration establishes reusable kernel-known memory regions.

options.label: Make every operation synchronous
options.explanation: Incorrect — The ring remains asynchronous.

options.label: Bypass all file permissions
options.explanation: Incorrect — I/O authorization still applies.

stem: Why should an event loop associate readiness with connection generation state rather than descriptor integer alone?

options.label: Descriptor integers are globally unique forever
options.explanation: Incorrect — They are small reusable process-local indexes.

options.label: epoll never reports disconnection
options.explanation: Incorrect — It can report hangup and error states.

options.label: A closed descriptor number can be reused for a different connection
options.explanation: Correct — Stale events keyed only by the integer can target the wrong object.

options.label: Generation state makes close unnecessary
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resources still need lifecycle cleanup.

stem: Why should a traditional signal handler call only async-signal-safe functions?

options.label: Handlers execute in a separate protected process
options.explanation: Incorrect — They interrupt a thread in the same process.

options.label: All libc functions are lock-free
options.explanation: Incorrect — Many use locks and mutable global state.

options.label: Signals arrive only between syscalls
options.explanation: Incorrect — They can interrupt user execution.

options.label: It may interrupt library code while internal state or locks are inconsistent
options.explanation: Correct — Reentering unsafe functions can deadlock or corrupt state.

stem: What security boundary does seccomp add that namespaces do not?

options.label: It restricts which system calls and arguments a process may use
options.explanation: Correct — Namespaces change resource views, while seccomp filters kernel entry points.

options.label: It creates a new PID numbering hierarchy
options.explanation: Incorrect — PID namespaces do that.

options.label: It sets memory.max
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cgroups enforce resource limits.

options.label: It provides filesystem encryption
options.explanation: Incorrect — Syscall filtering does not encrypt data.

stem: Why must cgroup v2 delegation restrict which controller files a tenant can modify?

options.label: Every controller is only cosmetic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Controllers change resource behavior.

options.label: Unsafe control could affect processes or resources outside the delegated subtree
options.explanation: Correct — Delegation preserves containment of administrative authority.

options.label: Tenants need host-root access to read metrics
options.explanation: Incorrect — Safe delegated interfaces avoid that.

options.label: Delegation creates a new user namespace automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — The mechanisms are separate.

stem: Why is a pidfd safer than retaining a numeric PID for later signaling?

options.label: It makes the process immortal
options.explanation: Incorrect — The process can still exit.

options.label: It grants permission to every signal
options.explanation: Incorrect — Normal permission checks remain.

options.label: It refers to the specific process object despite PID-number reuse
options.explanation: Correct — The handle avoids targeting a new process that inherited the number.

options.label: It is a virtual-memory address
options.explanation: Incorrect — It is a file descriptor.

stem: Why can an RCU read-side critical section avoid taking a conventional reader lock?

options.label: Writers mutate freed memory immediately
options.explanation: Incorrect — Deferred reclamation prevents that.

options.label: Readers never access shared data
options.explanation: Incorrect — They read shared published structures.

options.label: RCU makes CPUs sequential
options.explanation: Incorrect — It uses ordering and lifecycle rules on concurrent CPUs.

options.label: Writers defer reclamation until pre-existing readers pass a grace period
options.explanation: Correct — Readers can use an old version safely while updates publish a new one.

stem: What is the ABA problem in a compare-and-swap algorithm?

options.label: A value changes away and back, hiding intervening state from equality comparison
options.explanation: Correct — CAS sees the same bits even though object identity or history changed.

options.label: The compare operation is never atomic
options.explanation: Incorrect — CAS itself is atomic.

options.label: Two different addresses always compare equal
options.explanation: Incorrect — Equality depends on actual values.

options.label: A lock is held recursively
options.explanation: Incorrect — ABA is a lock-free validation issue.

stem: When is a relaxed atomic increment a suitable choice?

options.label: The counter publishes a fully initialized object
options.explanation: Incorrect — Publication needs release/acquire or stronger synchronization.

options.label: Only the count must be atomic, with no ordering of other data derived from it
options.explanation: Correct — Relaxed order preserves modification atomicity without synchronization edges.

options.label: The operation protects a non-atomic data structure
options.explanation: Incorrect — Atomic counter updates do not serialize other memory.

options.label: Every thread needs a global total order of all operations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Relaxed order does not provide that.

stem: A producer initializes an object then release-stores its pointer. What must the consumer use before reading fields?

options.label: A plain unsynchronized load
options.explanation: Incorrect — That lacks the required visibility edge.

options.label: A relaxed store to an unrelated variable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unrelated operations do not synchronize publication.

options.label: An acquire load that observes the published pointer
options.explanation: Correct — The pair makes preceding initialization visible.

options.label: A filesystem fsync
options.explanation: Incorrect — Storage durability is irrelevant to memory ordering.

stem: What extra reasoning aid does sequential consistency provide for atomics?

options.label: Every ordinary data race becomes safe
options.explanation: Incorrect — Non-atomic conflicting accesses remain invalid.

options.label: All operations execute on one CPU
options.explanation: Incorrect — The guarantee is semantic, not physical placement.

options.label: Caches are disabled
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hardware can use caches while preserving the model.

options.label: They appear in one global order consistent with each thread’s order
options.explanation: Correct — The model supplies a single interleaving for sequentially consistent actions.

stem: Why can padding two hot counters onto separate cache lines improve scalability?

options.label: It avoids coherence invalidations between independent writers
options.explanation: Correct — Each core can modify its own line.

options.label: It reduces the number of logical counters
options.explanation: Incorrect — The program still has two counters.

options.label: It guarantees both counters are atomic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Alignment does not itself add atomic semantics.

options.label: It eliminates virtual-address translation
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLBs remain involved.

stem: Why can migrating a worker without its memory reduce performance on NUMA hardware?

options.label: Remote memory is always inaccessible
options.explanation: Incorrect — It remains addressable through the interconnect.

options.label: The worker may perform higher-latency remote-node memory accesses
options.explanation: Correct — CPU and page placement become mismatched.

options.label: Migration clears the process address space
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU migration preserves the process mappings and their existing page placement.

options.label: NUMA nodes are filesystem directories
options.explanation: Incorrect — They are memory and CPU topology domains.

stem: Why does a concurrent tracing collector use write barriers?

options.label: Prevent the program from writing any heap field
options.explanation: Incorrect — Writes continue with added bookkeeping.

options.label: Make every object immutable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Collectors support mutable heaps.

options.label: Track pointer mutations that could otherwise hide live objects from the marker
options.explanation: Correct — Mutators run while the collector builds its reachability view.

options.label: Replace all root scanning
options.explanation: Incorrect — Roots still seed tracing.

stem: Why does G1 maintain remembered sets for heap regions?

options.label: Keep every region permanently live
options.explanation: Incorrect — Liveness is still traced.

options.label: Store compiled machine code only
options.explanation: Incorrect — They summarize heap references.

options.label: Disable object movement
options.explanation: Incorrect — G1 can evacuate live objects.

options.label: Find references into a region without scanning the entire heap
options.explanation: Correct — Cross-region pointer summaries bound collection work.

stem: What does a runtime safepoint provide during stack-sensitive GC work?

options.label: Thread states where roots and execution metadata can be inspected consistently
options.explanation: Correct — The runtime coordinates mutators at known recoverable locations.

options.label: A guarantee no thread will ever resume
options.explanation: Incorrect — Safepoints are temporary.

options.label: A durable filesystem checkpoint
options.explanation: Incorrect — They concern managed execution state.

options.label: A replacement for page tables
options.explanation: Incorrect — The OS still translates memory.

stem: Why do JIT runtimes use several compilation tiers?

options.label: Every tier targets a different filesystem
options.explanation: Incorrect — Tiers are compiler strategies.

options.label: Start quickly with cheap code, then optimize hot paths using profiles
options.explanation: Correct — Tiering balances startup cost and peak throughput.

options.label: Lower tiers cannot execute machine code
options.explanation: Incorrect — Baseline tiers often emit machine code.

options.label: Optimization requires no runtime observations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hotness and types often guide decisions.

stem: Why must optimized JIT code retain metadata for deoptimization and GC?

options.label: Machine code contains no values
options.explanation: Incorrect — Execution state holds program values.

options.label: Metadata makes speculation always correct
options.explanation: Incorrect — It enables recovery when speculation fails.

options.label: The runtime must reconstruct logical frames and locate live references
options.explanation: Correct — Optimized registers and stack slots differ from source-level state.

options.label: The kernel automatically rebuilds language frames
options.explanation: Incorrect — This is runtime-specific work.

options.explanation: Incorrect — Branch prediction and paging are separate.

options.explanation: Incorrect — Misprediction is handled within the CPU pipeline.
